Total sample.py calls: 110 of 120 (10 left, stopped with buffer).

Distinct restarts in answer: 8, split 4 (half 1) / 4 (half 2).
- H1: throw-in home @800 (o0); direct-FK home @1360 (o0); throw-in home @1853 (o0); direct-FK home @2878 (o0).
- H2: throw-in home @4220 (o0); direct-FK home @4469 (o0); direct-FK home @5170 (o1, shot); corner home @5286 (o0).
Match was Mainz(red,home) vs Dortmund(yellow,away); final 1:1 (Dortmund early goal ~2min, Mainz equalizer ~82min from an open-play header, not a restart).

Easy vs hard: Easy — the scoreboard game-clock tracked t almost exactly (clock_seconds ≈ t), which made time-anchoring and half boundaries trivial, and throw-ins/walled free-kicks were unambiguous when a frame happened to land on the execution (player ball-overhead, or ball+kicker+wall). Hard — with 120 samples over 5400s, coarse 80s sweeps almost never landed on the brief restart moment itself; they mostly caught broadcast cutaways (player close-ups, linesman flag, injuries) that signal a stoppage is NEAR but not its exact second, type, or which team. Pinning onset within 3s AND reading the taker's kit AND the 15s/30s outcome each cost several zoom calls, so I could only convert a handful. Distinguishing direct vs indirect FK and corner-vs-wide-FK from single frames was often impossible, and free-kick team was ambiguous when the frame showed a mixed cluster rather than the taker. Result skews entirely "home" because Mainz (chasing 0:1) took the attacking set-pieces I could positively identify; I surely missed many Dortmund throw-ins/FKs that fell between coarse samples.

The scoreboard's running game clock (≈ t in seconds) made time-anchoring reliable. Final answer and the full easy-vs-hard writeup have been relayed to the team lead.
